title: Data Structures & Algorithms
summary: Organizing data and stepping through it efficiently, measured with Big-O.
hook: Pick the container that makes your most common question cheap.

cards.q: Why do we measure algorithms with Big-O instead of seconds?
cards.a: It describes growth with input size, independent of hardware.

cards.q: Name five core data structures.
cards.a: Array, linked list, hash table, tree, graph (plus stack, queue, heap).

children.title: Complexity
children.summary: Big-O time and space, best/worst/amortized cases.
children.hook: How does the work grow if the input doubles?

cards.q: Order these: O(n log n), O(1), O(n²), O(log n), O(n).
cards.a: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²).

cards.q: What does amortized O(1) mean?
cards.a: Occasional expensive ops average out to constant cost per op over a sequence.

children.title: Big-O Notation
children.summary: Upper-bound growth rate as input size goes to infinity; constants drop.
children.hook: Big-O is the shape of the curve, not the speed of the car.

cards.q: Why do we drop constants?
cards.a: For large n, the growth shape dominates; constants depend on hardware anyway.

cards.q: Big-O of two nested loops over n?
cards.a: O(n²).

children.title: Amortized Analysis
children.summary: Averaging occasional expensive operations over many cheap ones, like dynamic array growth.
children.hook: Moving to a house twice as big: rare and painful, but cheap per year lived there.

cards.q: Why is appending to a dynamic array amortized O(1)?
cards.a: Copying happens rarely; with doubling, total copy work is about 2n for n appends.

cards.q: What growth factor makes that work?
cards.a: Any constant factor > 1, typically 1.5 or 2.

children.title: Recursion & Master Theorem
children.summary: Recurrences like T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n and how to solve them.
children.hook: Split the work, solve the halves, pay to combine: count the work per level × levels.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.
cards.a: O(n log n): n work per level, log n levels.

cards.q: What is the space cost of recursion?
cards.a: O(depth) call-stack frames.

children.title: Linear Structures
children.summary: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues and hash tables.
children.hook: Lined-up items: by position, by link, by last-in, first-in, or by key.

cards.q: Array vs linked list: tradeoffs?
cards.a: Array: O(1) index, slow middle inserts. Linked list: O(1) insert at a node, O(n) access.

cards.q: Which structure gives O(1) average lookup by key?
cards.a: A hash table.

children.title: Arrays & Strings
children.summary: Contiguous memory, O(1) index access, O(n) inserts in the middle.
children.hook: Numbered lockers in a row: jump straight to locker 57.

cards.q: Why is array access O(1)?
cards.a: Address = base + index × size, a single computation.

cards.q: Cost of inserting at index 0?
cards.a: O(n): every element shifts right.

children.title: Linked Lists
children.summary: Nodes with next pointers; O(1) insert at a known node, O(n) search.
children.hook: A treasure hunt: each clue points to the next.

cards.q: Reverse a linked list: describe the pointer moves.
cards.a: Walk with prev, cur: save next, point cur.next to prev, advance prev and cur.

cards.q: How do you detect a cycle?
cards.a: Floyd's tortoise and hare: a fast and a slow pointer meet if there's a cycle.

children.title: Stacks & Queues
children.summary: LIFO and FIFO; deques and monotonic stacks build on them.
children.hook: Stack of plates vs line at a coffee shop.

cards.q: Name a problem solved with a stack.
cards.a: Balanced parentheses, undo, or next-greater-element (monotonic stack).

cards.q: Implement a queue with two stacks: how?
cards.a: Push to an in-stack; to dequeue, if the out-stack is empty move everything over, then pop from out.

children.title: Hash Tables
children.summary: Hash keys to buckets for O(1) average get/put; handle collisions by chaining or probing.
children.hook: Coat check by ticket number: the number tells you exactly which hook.

cards.q: Chaining vs open addressing?
cards.a: Chaining keeps a list per bucket; open addressing probes for the next free slot.

cards.q: Why does load factor matter?
cards.a: Higher load means more collisions and slower ops; tables resize to keep it low.

children.title: Trees & Heaps
children.summary: Hierarchical structures for ordered data and priorities.
children.hook: A family tree: one root, branching down, no loops.

cards.q: Define height and depth of a tree.
cards.a: Depth: edges from root to a node. Height: longest path from a node down to a leaf.

cards.q: Why do balanced trees matter?
cards.a: They keep height O(log n), so operations stay O(log n).

children.title: Tree Traversals
children.summary: Pre-, in-, post-order DFS and level-order BFS.
children.hook: Pre: visit, then kids. In: left, me, right. Post: kids first. Level: floor by floor.

cards.q: Which traversal gives sorted order on a BST?
cards.a: In-order.

cards.q: Iterative in-order: what do you keep on the stack?
cards.a: The path of ancestors whose left subtrees you're still exploring; go left until null, pop, visit, go right.

children.title: Binary Search Trees
children.summary: Left < node < right; O(log n) operations when balanced (AVL, red-black).
children.hook: A guessing game: higher or lower at every node.

cards.q: How do you delete a node with two children?
cards.a: Replace it with its in-order successor (smallest in the right subtree), then delete the successor.

cards.q: What makes a BST degrade to O(n)?
cards.a: Inserting sorted data makes it a linked list.

children.title: Heaps & Priority Queues
children.summary: Array-backed complete trees with O(log n) push/pop and O(1) peek.
children.hook: A tournament bracket: the champion is always on top.

cards.q: How do you find the k largest items with a heap?
cards.a: Keep a min-heap of size k; push each item and pop when size exceeds k; the heap holds the k largest.

cards.q: Why is heapify O(n)?
cards.a: Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a little; the sum converges to O(n).

children.title: Tries
children.summary: Prefix trees for fast word and prefix lookups.
children.hook: Autocomplete as a tree of letters.

cards.q: What is the cost of inserting a word of length L?
cards.a: O(L).

cards.q: Name two problems tries are good for.
cards.a: Autocomplete/prefix search and word games like Boggle or word search.

children.title: Graphs
children.summary: Nodes and edges: modeling networks, dependencies and maps.
children.hook: Cities and roads: anything connected is a graph.

cards.q: Adjacency list vs matrix?
cards.a: List is compact for sparse graphs; matrix gives O(1) edge checks but O(V²) space.

cards.q: Directed vs undirected, weighted vs unweighted?
cards.a: Directed edges have a direction (follows); weighted edges have costs (distances).

children.title: BFS & DFS
children.summary: Breadth-first finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first explores fully.
children.hook: BFS: ripples in a pond. DFS: a maze runner who goes deep, then backtracks.

cards.q: Why does BFS give shortest paths in unweighted graphs?
cards.a: It explores in order of distance, so the first time it reaches a node is via the fewest edges.

cards.q: How do you avoid revisiting nodes?
cards.a: Keep a visited set and mark nodes when you enqueue/push them.

children.title: Shortest Paths
children.summary: Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford with negatives.
children.hook: Always expand the closest unsettled city next.

cards.q: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges?
cards.a: It finalizes a node assuming no later path can be cheaper; a negative edge breaks that.

cards.q: Dijkstra's complexity with a heap?
cards.a: O((V + E) log V).

children.title: Topological Sort
children.summary: Order a DAG so every edge points forward (Kahn's algorithm or DFS).
children.hook: Getting dressed: socks before shoes.

cards.q: Describe Kahn's algorithm.
cards.a: Queue all nodes with in-degree 0; pop one, output it, decrement neighbors' in-degree, enqueue any that hit 0.

cards.q: How does it detect a cycle?
cards.a: If fewer than V nodes are output, the rest are in a cycle.

children.title: Union-Find
children.summary: Disjoint sets with path compression and union by rank, near O(1) per op.
children.hook: Everyone points to their group's leader; merge by pointing one leader at another.

cards.q: What do path compression and union by rank each do?
cards.a: Path compression flattens the tree on finds; union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller.

cards.q: Name a problem union-find solves.
cards.a: Counting connected components, or detecting cycles in Kruskal's MST.

children.title: Techniques
children.summary: Reusable problem-solving patterns that turn brute force into efficient solutions.
children.hook: Recognize the shape of the problem, then reach for the matching tool.

cards.q: What's the first pattern you check when input is sorted?
cards.a: Two pointers or binary search.

cards.q: How do you spot a DP problem?
cards.a: Choices that overlap: the same subproblem gets recomputed, and the best answer builds from best sub-answers.

children.title: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
children.summary: Move two indices through a sequence to avoid nested loops.
children.hook: A caterpillar: the front stretches, the back catches up.

cards.q: When does a sliding window apply?
cards.a: Contiguous subarray/substring problems where expanding and shrinking keeps a running condition.

cards.q: Two-sum on a sorted array: how?
cards.a: Left at start, right at end; sum too small → move left up, too big → move right down.

children.title: Binary Search
children.summary: Halve the search space each step, including searching over the answer.
children.hook: Guess a number 1–100 in seven tries.

cards.q: What is the loop invariant?
cards.a: The answer, if it exists, is always within [lo, hi].

cards.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
cards.a: Search over possible answer values when you can test 'is x feasible?' and feasibility is monotonic.

children.title: Dynamic Programming
children.summary: Overlapping subproblems plus optimal substructure: memoize or build bottom-up.
children.hook: Write down answers to subproblems so you never solve the same one twice.

cards.q: Memoization vs tabulation?
cards.a: Memoization: top-down recursion with a cache. Tabulation: bottom-up filling a table.

cards.q: Define the state and transition for climbing stairs.
cards.a: dp[i] = ways to reach step i; dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].

children.title: Backtracking
children.summary: Build candidates step by step and undo choices that can't lead to a solution.
children.hook: Exploring a maze with chalk: mark, try, erase if it's a dead end.

cards.q: Sketch the backtracking template.
cards.a: choose → recurse → unchoose, with a base case that records a solution.

cards.q: How does pruning help?
cards.a: It cuts branches that can't succeed early, saving exponential work.

children.title: Greedy
children.summary: Take the locally best choice when it provably leads to a global optimum.
children.hook: Grab the best thing in front of you, when you can prove you'll never regret it.

cards.q: Give a problem where greedy works and one where it fails.
cards.a: Works: interval scheduling by earliest end. Fails: coin change with coins {1, 3, 4} for 6.

cards.q: How do you justify a greedy choice?
cards.a: An exchange argument: swapping any optimal solution's choice for the greedy one doesn't make it worse.

children.title: Sorting
children.summary: Ordering data: comparison sorts and their limits, plus linear-time special cases.
children.hook: Comparisons can only shrink possibilities so fast.

cards.q: Why can't comparison sorts beat O(n log n)?
cards.a: There are n! orderings and each comparison halves them at best: log₂(n!) ≈ n log n.

cards.q: What does stable mean?
cards.a: Equal elements keep their original relative order.

children.title: Merge & Quick Sort
children.summary: Divide and conquer: merge is stable O(n log n); quick is in-place with O(n²) worst case.
children.hook: Merge: split and zip. Quick: pick a pivot, throw smaller left, bigger right.

cards.q: Why pick a random pivot?
cards.a: To make the O(n²) worst case (sorted input with a fixed pivot) vanishingly unlikely.

cards.q: Space cost of merge sort?
cards.a: O(n) extra space for merging.

children.title: Counting & Radix Sort
children.summary: Beat O(n log n) when keys are small integers or fixed-width.
children.hook: Sorting mail into labeled cubbies instead of comparing letters.

cards.q: When does counting sort win?
cards.a: When the key range k is small relative to n: O(n + k).

cards.q: Why does radix sort need a stable inner sort?
cards.a: Each digit pass must preserve the order from earlier passes.
